notes.1: This question required candidates to recognise that the boiling point would be higher than the melting point and that pure substances tend to have sharp melting and boiling points rather than a range of values. All of the distractors were chosen with Distractor B being the most common.
notes.3: This question on diffusion required candidates to recognise that particles move, by diffusion, down a concentration gradient to form a homogenous mixture. A point in the gas jars where there are no NO particles or no air particles can therefore be eliminated as incorrect from the options. �PAGE�5
notes.4: This question discriminated well between the most and least able candidates, with many appearing to be guessing. All the distractors were equally chosen by the least able candidates.
notes.6: This question discriminated well between the most and least able candidates. Distractor C was the most common incorrect answer.
notes.10: Only a quarter of the candidates overall answered this correctly with a significant majority choosing Distractor C. The molecular formula gives the total number of each type of atom and so it was anticipated that candidates could count up each atom type even though options included some unfamiliar compounds.
notes.14: Few candidates chose Distractor B or Distractor D and so correctly identified the link between temperature and energy change. Distractor A was chosen by the majority of candidates showing a common confusion in this representation of exothermic and endothermic reactions.
notes.18: The correct answer was the least popular choice for this question. At this level candidates are required to know that redox reactions involve the gain or loss of oxygen. Reaction 1 was combustion which requires oxygen and reaction 2 was rusting which requires both water and oxygen.
notes.21: This was the least well answered question on the paper. Distractor D was the most common answer with candidates assuming that the Periodic Table places the elements in order of nucleon number rather than atomic number. Elements in Group VII have 7 outer shell electrons and form ions with a 1– charge.
notes.22: Although the stronger candidates tended to choose the correct answer more than any other option, weaker candidates tended to choose Distractor C showing recall of the trend in reactivity of Group I elements but not their physical properties.
notes.24: Weaker candidates appeared to be guessing with all the options frequently chosen. More able candidates had little problem with this question.
notes.25: Many candidates mistakenly assumed that helium has eight outer shell electrons rather than just two. Distractor A was the most common answer.
notes.26: Across all candidates all the options were commonly chosen with a preference for Distractor C by the less able candidates and Distractor A by the more able. It could help candidates to remember the order of reactivity of the elements by using a mnemonic generator. The more reactive elements such as aluminium are more difficult to extract from their ores and require electrolysis rather than simple reduction using carbon or carbon monoxide.
notes.29: The four options were equally chosen by the weaker candidates, whereas the stronger candidates overall had little difficulty with this question. �PAGE�6
notes.30: This was a challenging question and fewer than a third of the candidates answered correctly. Candidates were required to recall that clean, dry air is 21 per cent oxygen and that oxygen reacts readily, when heated with copper. Many candidates assumed no reaction would occur and chose Distractor D.
notes.31: Distractor A was chosen by more than third of the candidates overall. In common with the theory papers, candidates often confuse the origin and adverse effects of common air pollutants.
notes.35: This question discriminated well between the candidates, with weaker candidates appearing to have been guessing. �PAGE�7
notes.general_comments:
Candidates found this to be an accessible paper overall with most questions showing good discrimination
between candidates. Overall candidates found Question 9, 17, 27, 33 and 39 to have the least challenge.
Question 1, 10, 18, 21, 22, 26 and 30 were most demanding.
The reactivity and properties of metals and alloys were not well recalled.
In common with previous years, questions on organic chemistry were found to be more challenging, as a
whole, compared with other topics.
